topic: The Solar Boom vs Coal Bust
description: A high-contrast timeline of how global solar installations surged while coal power generation and new coal builds stalled—capturing the pivot from fossil expansion to clean-energy scale.
youtube_description:
⚡️ Solar went from niche to global system-scale—and coal funding started to look like a shrinking tailwind.

In this chart-race style video, we stack four real-world proxies over time:
1) cumulative solar CapEx (scale up),
2) cumulative coal CapEx (scale down),
3) coal generation index (demand pressure),
4) solar GW added per year (momentum).

⏱️ Chapters
00:00 — The pivot: why solar suddenly breaks the ceiling
02:10 — 2010–2013: cost curves + policy + grid ambition
06:30 — 2014–2016: the boom becomes unavoidable
10:15 — 2017–2019: coal expansion stops feeling safe
13:50 — 2020–2022: energy shocks + renewables accelerate
17:40 — 2023–2025: the new normal—solar keeps scaling

What you’re watching is the same story told two ways: money flowing to solar hardware while new coal investment stalls, even as coal generation flattens and drifts downward.

instagram_caption:
🚀 The Solar Boom vs Coal Bust: the money trail that changed the grid.

For years, coal felt like the default answer—steady, scalable, “always-on.” But the turning point wasn’t just policy or headlines. It was the math: costs dropping for solar hardware and the resulting wave of real construction spending. In our timeline, solar CapEx (cumulative) rises from ~$70B in 2006 to ~$2200B by 2025, a multi-decade acceleration that flips the investment gravity.

Now watch the other side. Coal power CapEx (cumulative) peaks around the mid/late 2010s (about ~$460B by 2014–2015) and then trends down—falling to ~$300B by 2025. That’s a major narrative shift: even when coal generation doesn’t collapse overnight, the willingness to fund new builds starts shrinking.

Here’s the drama in the middle: coal generation (index, 2006=100) grows slightly through the 2010s (to ~115 by 2019), then flattens and eases downward—dropping to ~104 by 2025. Meanwhile, solar installations keep compounding—annual solar additions go from ~15 GW (2006) to ~285 GW (2025). In a chart race, that’s how you get the “skyrocket vs crushed” look: install rates surge while investment momentum turns cautious.

The result? A transition that doesn’t just look green—it looks profitable, scalable, and faster to deploy. The era of “coal first” keeps losing ground, not in one single year, but across dozens of data points.

👇 Which would you rather track next in a chart race: EV charging buildout vs fossil refineries, or battery storage vs peaker plants?
facebook_caption:
The global energy transition can be visualized as a funding tug-of-war. From 2006 to 2025, cumulative solar power capital expenditure rises sharply (from about $70B to about $2200B in estimated totals), reflecting sustained deployment and system-scale cost improvements. Over the same period, cumulative coal power capital expenditure trends downward (from about $340B to about $300B), showing reduced appetite for new coal capacity.

The operational picture mirrors the investment shift. Coal generation remains relatively stable through the 2010s (coal generation index increases from 100 in 2006 to roughly 115 by 2019), before gradually easing to around 104 by 2025. At the same time, solar additions accelerate from roughly 15 GW added annually in 2006 to about 285 GW annually by 2025.

This creates the clearest “chart-race” dynamic: solar grows with compounding annual buildouts, while coal sees investment compression and slow normalization rather than an immediate collapse.

If you want, I can generate a follow-up comparison (storage vs peaker plants; natural gas vs renewables; grid buildout vs transmission bottlenecks).
threads_caption:
Solar vs coal is basically the ultimate chart-race story. 👀

Cumulative solar CapEx goes from ~$70B (2006) to ~$2200B (2025), while coal CapEx fades from ~$340B to ~$300B. Even though coal generation only drifts down slowly (index ~115 in 2019 → ~104 by 2025), solar additions keep compounding: ~15 GW/yr (2006) → ~285 GW/yr (2025).

So the “crush” isn’t always instant—it often looks like money momentum changing first.
